name: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
title: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
answer: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the documents, conversations and evidence that show how an AI system reaches its outputs and where its limits lie. It includes model cards, validation reports, data lineage summaries, performance metrics, known failure modes and plain language descriptions of assumptions. The work sits inside governance and fiduciary risk because a firm must be able to justify decisions made with or about AI to supervisors, auditors, customers and boards. It is not only a technical exercise, it is a translation exercise between data science, legal, compliance and business teams.

sections.body: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the documents, conversations and evidence that show how an AI system reaches its outputs and where its limits lie. It includes model cards, validation reports, data lineage summaries, performance metrics, known failure modes and plain language descriptions of assumptions. The work sits inside governance and fiduciary risk because a firm must be able to justify decisions made with or about AI to supervisors, auditors, customers and boards. It is not only a technical exercise, it is a translation exercise between data science, legal, compliance and business teams.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a model inventory or registry that records every model in use, its owner, its version and its purpose. Documentation lives in version controlled repositories, often alongside code, with links to data lineage tools, feature stores and monitoring dashboards. Explanation methods such as SHAP or LIME may run on separate compute, and their outputs are stored with the model version they describe. Access controls, audit logs and retention policies are part of the infrastructure because regulators and clients may ask who saw what and when.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical process starts with an inventory and a risk tiering, so that high impact models receive deeper explanation than low impact ones. Teams then produce documentation that states the model's purpose, training data, validation results, limitations and the business decision it supports. They test explanations for stability, check that they match known behavior, and have legal and compliance review the language before it goes to a regulator or client. The final step is often a dry run or a question and answer session, because an explanation that cannot survive follow up questions is not finished.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on provenance, confidentiality and accuracy. A firm must know whether it has the right to use the training data, whether client data appears in outputs, and whether disclosure would reveal trade secrets or personal information. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, which shows that unclear model claims can become disputes over liability, discrimination or contract terms. Provenance records, consent agreements, bias testing and clear statements of uncertainty are common controls, and regulators increasingly expect them to be produced on request.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more standardized disclosure formats, more automated documentation pipelines and more demand for continuous evidence rather than one time reports. Regulators are moving toward examining AI systems in the same way they examine financial models, with periodic validation and clear ownership. Clients are asking for plain language explanations of how automated decisions affect them, and for a route to challenge those decisions. The direction is toward traceable, versioned explanations that can be updated as models change, not static documents written once.
